speechtext:

subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS AT INCO-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE EFFECTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we are only one week into the third session of the thirtieth parliament and I see that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Transport are absent. My question is to a minister who is in the House, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and it concerns the economic devastation that is occurring in my constituency and in Sudbury as a result of the INCO lay-offs. Now that both labour and management have shot down the minister's idea of "fair shares of misery", policies of work sharing, will he tell the House what further steps he has in mind to make sure our communities can stay on their feet?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bud Cullen (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: LAY-OFFS AT INCO-GOVERNMENT MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE EFFECTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at a time when a problem such as this

October 26, 1977
Oral Questions
exists, it seems to me inappropriate not to examine all of the avenues which might be of assistance to those who are affected by the lay-off. That is precisely why we held meetings yesterday dealing not only with the Sudbury, Ontario situation, but also that in Thompson, Manitoba, the idea was in fact not shot down. They indicated that the problem was not of a temporary nature, knew that the work-sharing program would not be applicable on a long-term basis, and therefore not too much time was spent on the work-sharing aspect.
We indicated both to management and to union the full resources which would be available. The union leadership were of a mind that we were jumping a bridge too soon, if you will. They wanted to pursue with management the avenues that might be open to head off, or at least to ameliorate, the lay-off. I think that should be encouraged in order to see what can be done on a union-management basis. In the event that that is not successful or totally successful, then I think it is incumbent upon governments at both levels to do what they can to ameliorate the situation so far as those who are laid off are concerned.

speechtext:

In the light of the experience we are living in the mining industry and considering the concrete proof of the lack of a long term industrial policy, and given that, as confirmed today by the company, Noranda Mines will have to invite its employees to take a prolonged holiday during the Christmas period, which causes some concern to the mining industry in Quebec, would the minister be in a position to tell what kind of communication he had with this Quebec mining company and can he assure the House that we shall not have the kind of lay-offs we have just experienced in Ontario.

speechtext: -I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if he is aware that at the meeting which took place yesterday INCO said that not only will it proceed with its announced layoffs but that, quite possibly, there would be further layoffs early in 1978. We have not rejected that possibility; we have discussed it with the company, but at the present time this does not seem to be the solution to the problem.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege which relates to an answer given to a question this afternoon by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). The Minister of Finance was asked by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) whether the government is going to take action on a request which it had from the government of Newfoundland to impose a tariff on imports of fluorspar into Canada because of a decision by Alcan to close the fluorspar mine at St. Lawrence, Newfoundland. As I recall it, the minister said that he had received no such letter or request, but that he would consider it if he did receive such a letter.
That is a misstatement of fact, I believe, Mr. Speaker, inadvertent I am sure. I raised this question last night. On July 21 a letter was sent to the then minister of industry, trade and commerce, the present Minister of Finance, by the government of Newfoundland requesting that either a tariff be imposed on imported fluorspar or quotas imposed. This matter was debated last night. As reported at page 276 of yesterday's Hansard, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Loiselle), replying to me last night, said this:
I should also like to advise that the question of the imposition of a Canadian tariff on the importation of fluorspar is a matter for the consideration of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien). In that regard, my minister sent him a copy of Mr. Hickman's letter and his reply for his review.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, since July 21 or a few days thereafter, unless the post office has failed completely, or since October 11 in any event, this request has been before the Government of Canada. I bring this matter up because I think the minister has misstated the facts, and would he clear it up for me?

The House resumed, from Tuesday, October 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Dawson for an address to Her Majesty the Queen in reply to the speech at the opening of the session; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Malone (p. 226).

Mr. Speaker, to conclude my remarks from last evening, I would simply suggest that for a number of people, and especially for members of Frenchspeaking minorities outside Quebec, the most significant proposal in the Speech from the Throne, as read by Her Majesty, certainly was the government's intent to amend the BNA Act by enshrining linguistic rights in the constitution. The only language rights of sorts that have been included in the constitution since 1867 are those of the English-speaking minority in Quebec. And ever since 1971, this government's position has always been that our constitution should be amended to include language rights as well for the French-speaking minorities outside Quebec. Because since Confederation, when the existing agreement was prepared and enacted by the British Parliament, French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec have not really had an opportunity to participate in the preparation of that agreement. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I fully support the government's intention to introduce such amendments to the Constitution. This in my view is a matter of basic justice. Francophones outside Quebec have a right to such a constitutional guarantee. In my province, there is a statute on official languages but it is only an act of legislature. To us the significance of having that written into the Constitu-

October 26, 1977
tion would be a basic thing, and I hope the government succeed in getting such a constitutional amendment.
I would repeat that this position was not taken by the federal government on November 15 last or after the enactment of Bill 101 in Quebec. Rather, it has been the position of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the federal government since the Victoria Charter in 1971.

Mr. Speaker, firstly I should like to compliment the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I thought they did a remarkably fine job and I would hate to put them down or let them feel dismayed by the remark which is often heard around this House, that a person's maiden speech is frequently the best speech they ever make. It would be hard to improve on the ones they made. A maiden speech is one that a person sometimes spends half their life preparing to give. I know as a fact that after I made mine I wondered where I had found those wonderful phrases which I had in that speech. I heard some of them the other day. They were very fine speeches indeed.
I should also like to pay tribute to Her Majesty who lent the throne speech a distinction and attractiveness that it had in no other respect except in its reading.
As a defence critic for the official opposition I do not get many opportunities to speak on defence, and I usually take advantage of the throne speech or the budget speech to set out the party's views about our defence forces. However, the speech given the other night by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) appeared to be a budget speech in every regard except that it did not allow six days' debate. In every other regard it was a budget speech. He was aware of the fact that there should be six days of debate. Therefore he sneaked it into the middle of the throne speech.
Canada is unfortunate in that the government assumes no responsibility for reporting to the House or for reporting to Canadian people in regard to what it is doing with taxpayers' moneys, and its future plans. This is particularly the case in regard to the Department of National Defence. I can hardly recall the last speech of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) on defence. It has been at the instigation of the opposition that there have been debates or major speeches relating to defence. There was one exception to that, and that is when the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) made a statement on motions concerning the long-range patrol aircraft. That led to a lively afternoon of debate. Unfortunately this is the way it is in the Parliament of Canada governed by Trudeau liberals.
If the government is unwilling to explain what it is doing and what it proposes to do in these areas, then it is up to the opposition to force the government to explain itself. That is why I am taking this opportunity to talk about defence. The cornerstones of Canada's defence are alliances. Canada is not
October 26, 1977

very large, and there is already one Switzerland in the world. Therefore, we must have alliances or we cannot maintain neutrality. Even the New Democratic Party would agree that any country in this world today either needs to be well armed or it needs to have alliances. We are fortunate in our alliances.
I miss the NDP defence critic who was in the last parliament. He was defeated, but he seemed to have an interest in defence. At the present time that party has alternating critics who show up at defence committee meetings. The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) thinks we should withdraw from NORAD. The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) thinks we should withdraw from NATO. The hon. member who most often shows up thinks we should withdraw from everything. Given that type of input from a political party, they are not normally missed. The NDP party has no interest in defence, but its former critic kept the party honest; I would like to see them appoint someone permanently as their defence critic soon.
Our alliances are in relatively good shape, although NATO has a considerable amount of difficulty in regard to the standardization of equipment.
At this point I should like to return to the Minister of National Defence who has recently completed a trip to Norway. I would have liked to have seen an official press release from the minister's office on this subject, however, all we seem to receive from the minister's office on these trips is trivia. There was one exception to that in regard to the Norway trip. I understand the minister commented upon the difficulty of fulfilling the role of the ace force in Norway. Norway is unwilling to allow the basing or prepositioning of troops on her soil in peacetime. The Minister of National Defence has finally discovered this situation and realizes now that it is unlikely Canada would be able to land a force there and supply a force with any expectation of overcoming any opposition whatsoever.
At first the minister thought we might be letting our troops in for another Hong Kong experience; but I expect the bureaucrats, who make so much of the defence policy for Canada, convinced him that that was not the party line and he agreed with this rather foolish setup which is in existence at the present time. This forced the minister into another step, and that was asking Norwegians for naval assistance in order for us to get equipment over to our forces which, in the outbreak of war, would be marooned in Norway. Why do we not have our own ships to take our supplies, if that ever comes about? The truth is that, under the Trudeau government, supplying ships for our navy was considered to be a waste of money. Since the days when the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) first took office, there has not been a single keel laid down for a major Canadian vessel. We have had four vessels finished during his tenure, because he could not do anything to stop it. They have gone into service with the fleet.
It will be many, many years before the St. Laurent class of destroyer can be replaced. If the government started right now to move toward replacing the St. Laurent class of ship, that ship will be 28 years of age when replaced. It is a miracle to
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
the world that a Canadian vessel could last for 28 years in service. I recall someone saying that that class must have been a good class. We need a replacement for the St. Laurent class, but not as badly as the government needs a replacement of the St. Laurent class of Liberal politicians that we used to have.
I should like to refer to modern weapons. It is unfortunate we hear nothing about them from the Department of National Defence. The Minister referred to one such weapon yesterday as an enhanced radiation warhead and not a neutron bomb. One would expect an advertising agency to come out with the notion that increasing the radiation of a warhead enhances it somehow or other. Yesterday the minister waxed quite lyrical about the fact that it was a beautiful, enhanced radiation warhead! Combined with the cruise missile it is a weapon similar to the B-ls of World War II. It is very cheap, flies at a high speed, and with terrain guidance systems it would be almost impossible to shoot down or to knock down in any way. It can come in under radar, and our allies in western Europe are keen to have it.
If the neutron bomb is put on a cruise missile, one can understand what would happen. The cruise missile would fly under the radar and drop the neutron bomb, with its enhanced radiation warhead. This bomb can destroy people without tanks and within houses. It kills people, and it does not kill them in a very clean method. It is not a weapon we are particularly fond of, and the biggest danger about the neutron bomb is that it will lower the nuclear threshhold in western Europe. Perhaps some featherheaded person, or a person who might not keep cool under stress, might not consider the fact that the weapon he is using is a nuclear weapon. If he attempted to use such a warhead, that might inadvertently start a nuclear war. That is what 1 meant by lowering the nuclear threshhold.
Our allies in western Europe have asked the United States not to bargain away the cruise missile as part of the plan to get a Russian agreement as to the limitation of arms.
As has been well publicized, we have rented some tanks from the Germans. This will increase the fire power, the credibility and the mobility of our troops which were withdrawn from the central front in Europe and put into the reserves several years ago. I would appreciate a statement from the minister in the near future as to whether we are likely to move our brigade forward again now that we have some modern tanks.
At this time I would like to say something about the bad habit which the minister and the department have of making their very best case for the present situation at every opportunity. I attended a meeting of NATO parliamentarians recently and found, as I read over the general report on the security of the alliance, a section where Canada was mentioned in rather glowing terms. 1 knew that NATO would be pleased that the Liberals have adopted the Conservative suggestion concerning the re-equipment of our forces for which we have been plugging for so long, and have started to plan the re-equipping, but
294

October 26, 1977
The Address-Mr. McKinnon
they tend to spoil it for me when they use puffery to express what is supposed to be a factual statement. I found the following statement in the general report of the alliance concerning Canada. It says:
The decision has been taken to re-equip the Canadian forces with 128 German Leopard C-I main battle tanks. By mid 1979, the armoured strength of the Canadian Forces in Europe will have been increased from two tank squadrons to three with a total of 57 gun tanks and 8 specialist tanks.
That sounds pretty simple. It sounds as if we are going to put in 128 tanks and that we will increase our forces from two squadrons to three. That is what it says. I went to see the person who wrote this and said to him, "Thank you very much for your kind remarks about Canada. It was very heart warming to read them. Who wrote this?" He said, "Well, as a matter of fact, it was your Department of National Defence". So I started looking for the fine print. I had not realized that they would tell them that we would re-equip the Canadian forces with 128 German Leopard tanks when what we are talking about is tanks for both NATO and Canada. The three squadrons that they talk about will not be three squadrons in Germany, despite the fact that the statement says that the Canadian Forces in Europe will have been increased from two tank squadrons to three. They will have the reserve tanks for an extra squadron put into Germany and left there.
The truth of the matter was explained by General Dextraze, the recent chief of defence staff, on January 13, 1977, when he spoke at the Conference of Defence Associations. He said:
... A third squadron of tanks and a fourth battery of Mt09's will be located in Europe. Personnel to man these will come from Canada annually, for certain training exercises and in time of emergency as part of the Canadian Forces Europe augmentation plan.
The current thinking in NATO is that there will be no augmentation, that the only likely enemy there, the Warsaw Pact countries, are not likely to have a build-up before they move and we will have no time for augmentation at all. That is the modern thinking about it. Canadians are trying to con them, as this government does so often, that they will put more over there than in fact will be the case.
I should like to talk for a few minutes about standardization and the desperate feeling that many of us who have the interest of NATO at heart have about standardization. I knew well a general who was placed in charge of standardization in Brussels. He said it was the most discouraging job he had during his entire service, to try to make effective the standardization plans for NATO.
A startling example of this was last summer when the Germans and the Americans decided that they would standardize their main battle tanks and they would have a competition to decide which tank was the better tank, following which both countries would accept that tank. The Germans put up their Leopard II, the one that the government did not seem to realize was going to be produced when they ordered the obsolescent Leopard I. The Leopard II was sent to the United States for the competition and, according to most neutral observers, it emerged as the superior tank. All of a sudden what was thought to be an iron clad agreement became loose and we heard about a compromise solution. They would take

the Leopard II tank and the American gas turbine motor, which appeared to be a very good motor.
Things went on a little farther, and finally the word came out, I think it was in August, that the entire deal was off. The Americans were going to build their tank, the Germans were going to build their tank, and they would not have the same gun, the same motor, the same armour, or anything that was the same. What this means to a country that is out shopping for equipment, as Canada is, is a disaster. If we buy the German, which we are going to do-and unfortunately we are buying the one which will be replaced by the Leopard II some three or four years from now-we will be limited to working in that sector of Europe where maintenance is possible for Leopard tanks. It will not be in the American sector, it will have to be near the Germans or near the other nations which are buying the German tank as their main battle tank.
We are trying to rush through our speeches today to make room for others. I have a great deal more that I would like to say, and there are some things that I simply must review in general. We will soon be buying new fighter aircraft. The argument is just starting. The Canadian government has asked for applications from six different firms. I would only submit that I hope they have kept their options open to the possibility of buying two different types of aircraft. Our roles demand it. One is for aircraft to support NORAD, which is totally different than the other to support our ground support role in Germany, which the F-104 is doing at present.
If we end up with a single aircraft, we will have to apply to NATO to have the role of our airforce in Germany changed, because certainly an aircraft that would be able to carry out the NORAD role in North America could not begin to carry out our support role in Germany. That, unfortunately, is what we did with the F-104. It is a 1,500 mile an hour fighter that we put into a 600 mile an hour job. Having an F-104 in a support role is not cost effective, but that is what happens if you do not know what you are doing when you start out to buy aircraft. I hope that with regard to this aircraft the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce will not have everything to say about it. I know that offset work is important to Canadian industry.
Something that is very important to Canadians is that there be a good component of defence requirement in the fighter plane that is eventually chosen. We ended up with the F-5 because the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce wanted it, not the forces. We do not want that to happen again. I will only say one other thing about fighter aircraft. I am baffled how we managed to get the French to try to get our contracts when the know how much we want offset work. I have never heard Dussault or any other French company from France offering anyone offset work on fighter aircraft, and I would be amazed if they offered it here.
I would like to run over quickly what will happen with our equipment under this minister, who I think was rather lucky when he came here after the hon. member for Winnipeg South had managed to get the increased equipment budget. The new minister came along to spend it.
October 26, 1977

We will have the first long range patrol aircraft, about which there was a great deal of dispute a year ago, in May of 1980. The Leopard II tank is the first piece of new equipment to come as of July, 1978, a year from now. The new fighter aircraft will come in 1981, four years from now, and while we may want 125 to 150 of those, we will get ten or 15 a year. The program is to run for ten long years, so the airforce should not think they will be flying new aircraft early in the 1980's because the last ones will be arriving only in the 1990's. As for ships, we have a press leak from the minister's office which mentions 1985, but I am rather skeptical that we will have any by that time.
I will only say to our friends in the services that I am glad that we are moving in the right direction and that re-equipment has started, but this government has left us so far behind before it made a move that, despite the fact that two years ago it started to re-equip the forces, the only evidence of it in the hands of the troops in the major equipments of tanks, ships and planes, is that we have 35 tanks, rented from the Germans.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the past few days we have been speaking about changing circumstances in Canada, changes in the economy and changes in the lifestyles and attitudes of Canadians.
We have talked about the need for a new spirit among Canadians in order to reach a shared appreciation of our current problems and to reach a shared agreement on how these problems should be attacked. We need this co-operative spirit to deal with national unity. We need it to deal with unemployment. We need it in connection with crime and social problems. We need it to manage our energy resources and to make the best use of our food and agriculture resources.
I believe this is a crucial time for Canada's food industry. The past 32 years since the end of the Second World War have brought great changes to every sector. With the changes in the food and agricultural industry have come uncertainties. Consumers wonder what will happen to food prices next year. They wonder about nutrition and food additives. Food processors and retailers wonder about what will happen to their labour costs, what new technologies they will have to adapt to, and whether Canadian eating habits will change appreciably. Farmers wonder whether land prices will continue to rise and whether the prices for their commodities will justify paying more for farmland and for farm inputs.
Everyone wants to know what direction further changes in the food industry will take. But I believe we must take another approach to this uncertainty and concern. We must ask ourselves not only what direction developments in the food and agricultural industry will take, but also what direction we want them to take. We need to shape our agricultural policies with a clear idea of the potential of the industry and how that potential should be employed.
It is this approach that the government is taking in developing a food strategy for Canada. We are not saying that our
The Address-Mr. Whelan
current policies are not doing a good job. We are saying that we need a longer term plan for the food and agricultural industry. In making this plan we are asking for co-operation from everyone involved. The government has taken the lead in setting out the basic principles of the strategy. We are undertaking discussions among the federal departments and provincial departments and agencies to find ways to improve our services to producers and consumers and to build a stronger food industry.
In addition, as I announced last week, we have invited a number of major organizations within the industry to submit briefs on their responses to the white paper, "A Food Strategy for Canada". National organizations representing farmers, fishermen, processors, distributors, retailers and consumers will be presenting their opinions in December to a panel of ministers, including myself, who are working on the food strategy. We are looking forward to a frank public discussion with these organizations. While time and space have limited the number of groups invited to the December meeting, we are inviting all groups in the industry to make submissions. The government will consider the additional submissions at the National Food Conference which we will be holding next February.
Last week I announced some majors changes in the organization of my department. These were not changes just for the sake of change. It is a new look for the Department of Agriculture. It is also a new feeling about how the department can best do its job and how it can efficiently serve the total food industry, from the farmer's field to the consumer's dinner table.
All the attention which has been directed toward me as a farmer advocate, and all the department's work to assist the farmer seem to have blocked out in many people's minds the fact that the Department of Agriculture works for the consumer too. All the unheralded work we do with grading, inspection, food research, consumer advice on nutrition and so on, serves the general public. Our efforts to stabilize farm income and provide new technology in improved farm management benefits the consumer, and much more than he realizes.
As I said earlier in this House today, the research people in the Department of Agriculture and the farmers of Canada are the envy of the world. We farm in the northern hemisphere, and no other country in the northern hemisphere is as productive per man. We export much of our produce on the world market. In cereal grains alone we produce enough for our 24 million population and our livestock industry, which in turn in dollar volume is greater than the grain industry. We export enough for another 80 million people. No other country in the world exports such a high percentage of its production of cereal grains, which is close to 74 per cent.
On the subject of reorganization, hon. members will recall that the Speech from the Throne promised that the views of producers, consumers and processors will be adequately represented on marketing boards and agencies so that they can operate more efficiently. In this regard I will be making an announcement in the near future concerning changes in the

The Address-Mr. Whelan
make-up of the National Farm Products Marketing Council. These changes will be in harmony with the commitment of the government to ensure fair and equitable representation of all viewpoints in the supervision of national marketing boards.
Some of the changes which have been made have made farmers more efficient, but they have also left them more vulnerable to forces beyond their control. That is why farmers are concerned about the instability of prices. Farmers are not the only ones who suffer as a result of instability in agriculture. What about processors? What happens in the meat packing industry when the number of hogs coming to market drops by 20 per cent in one year? The instability of farmers' incomes is also quickly transmitted to those Canadians who supply farmers with building materials, machinery, fertilizer, and a long list of other goods and services. This is what has happened in the hog industry in Canada. Because there have been no government programs, farmers decided over a period of a year and a half or so that they should discontinue producing hogs. This year we will not be self-sufficient in hogs.
Shame!

We will be a net importer of pork this year. Some people would say that that is because of marketing boards, but the province from which the hon. member who is yelling "shame" comes has no marketing board and no supply management, and that province has decreased production. That decision was made in that province. We know what happens when that takes place. We know that packing plants close down and jobs are lost. However, that is the decision the farmers themselves made. For the last nine years farmers have made money out of pork production in Canada. There has never been a year in which they have not showed profit.
They made a decision which caused the closing down of packing plants, and we are now importing pork from the United States. We are still fulfilling our export orders and the commitments we have made to such countries as Japan. The producers signed contracts. They knew what they were going to get.
The hon. member who is making comments would be interested to know what Mr. Child, the manager of Burns, said yesterday in Montreal and what he said a week ago in Edmonton. He said that pork producers in the province of Alberta should look to the dairy producers in that province. Modern plants have been kept up to snuff, and dairy producers are getting a proper return. Mr. Child concluded by saying that they have a supply management system in the fluid milk industry in the province of Alberta which is superior to anything in the hog industry. All the plants are flourishing and are as modern as can be. They are going full speed ahead, but in the pork industry packing plants have closed down, and not because of anything the government has done. The consumer has been affected by this. Fluctuations in bacon prices have taken place. Packing plants have not been modernized, but the opposite has been the case in the dairy industry.
I think we must be realistic and recognize that, when prices are high, producers expand their operations and new farm
{Mr. Whelan.]
enterprises start. In periods of lower farm incomes producers are forced to cut back or perhaps even to get out of the business. This movement of physical and human resources in and out of food production adds to the cost of producing food. Ultimately the consumer pays the higher cost. We must also consider the cost of unused capacity or adjustment which is needed at the food processing level.
The whole food and agricultural industry stands to gain from increased stability down on the farm. That is why stabilization has been a priority policy of this government. We have supported the concept of marketing boards. We have amended and updated the Agricultural Stabilization Act. Since the Agricultural Stabilization Act was revised in 1975, we have paid out $100 million to improve producer returns.
We have set up the western grain stabilization program. There is every indication of a substantial payment to western grain farmers this year under this program. Just last session we presented the Advance Payments for Crops Act which stabilizes returns on storable crops by helping farmers even out their marketings throughout the crop year. That is something new that farmers who produce cash crops in eastern Ontario have been able to take advantage of.
There is a long list of programs that support and stabilize the Canadian food and agricultural industry. The federal government spent more than $56 million last year on crop insurance. This year our contribution to crop insurance is expected to reach $75.5 million. Under the domestic feed grain program, we have set up a $14.5 million budget in Ontario for feed freight adjustment programs that encourage farmers to build permanent on-farm storage for grain and silage, and to instal grain handling and drying devices and feed preparation equipment. Ontario has signed that agreement. We are working with the province of Ontario and many farmers from Elgin County, for instance, have taken advantage of this program. At least 50 farmers in the community around that of the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) have taken advantage of this. He must have done a good advertising job of the wonderful program we have developed for farmers in the area.
We are working hard with the Quebec government which has been reluctant to sign this agreement. They have dilly-dallied. The Minister of Agriculture for Ontario signed it months ago, but Quebec is blaming us for not going ahead. We have been funding forage transportation assistance programs in co-operation with Ontario and Saskatchewan to help livestock producers who have suffered unusual crop losses because of bad weather.
Canadian farmers operate in the toughest climate in North America. We make the comparison with the United States so often and so easily, but I must tell you that other countries in the northern hemisphere come here to learn how we produce so much food in this northern, cold country called Canada. They know our extreme climatic conditions, yet none of them approach our productivity. Our programs have to be as good and in many cases better than those of our neighbour to the
October 26, 1977

south. The United States enjoys an ideal climate for food production. An examination of the programs we have put in place shows we have provided superior programs when they were needed to give assurance of adequate supplies of wholesome food from farms that must contend with problems posed by our northerly climate.
The former secretary of agriculture of the United States was in Ottawa the day before yesterday. He withdrew a lot of programs, and now the present Secretary of Agriculture has been forced to put them back because of threats of strikes etc. by farmers as a result of their losses.
A United States team is in Canada at present studying our crop insurance program because United States farmers do not enjoy the kind of protection our farmers have. They do not have the tremendous Western Grain Stabilization Act that protects our farmers. As I said already, it appears there will be a substantial payment under that program. Through our Agricultural Stabilization Act we can cover any commodity as required, including grains grown outside the Canadian Wheat Board area and livestock across the country. The United States has no stabilization plan like this to cover livestock production and give the livestock producers the protection they need in world markets, and they are under tremendous pressure to introduce programs such as we have in this country.
The federal dairy policy recognizes the challenge faced by dairy farmers through short summers and long winters. No other country in the world houses its dairy cattle as long as we must. We have overcome this problem through the application of science and such things as genetic breeding. We have some of the best dairy cattle in the world, and other countries come here to study our methods. Cattle are the best producers of highly nutritious food, particularly the Holstein cattle in Canada. Let no one say that any dairy policy, provincial or federal, has caused inefficiency in the dairy industry.
The two-price wheat system in this country protects both consumers and producers in a way not found in the rest of North America or maybe even in the world. However, there is more to be done. Our first priority now is to reach an agreement with the provinces to harmonize all the stabilization programs for various commodities that are produced and marketed nationally.
The danger exists that some provincial stabilization programs may lead to production shifts against the comparative advantage of producing commodities in one area of the country over another. Recently the Minister of Agriculture for Brazil was here and he told me he was concerned that if one commodity goes down in price while he has made commitments to world markets and, as a result, producers switch to another crop on their own, he has to be able to stop such a switch.
In western Canada pork producers reduced production by 46 per cent on their own. They were still making money, but it was easier to sell grain than to take care of hogs. I realize that, but it does not help the packing industry or employment in different parts of the country. It does not help our balance of trade either to spend more money outside the country for pork
The Address-Mr. Whelan
than ever before. We have to import pork because we are not self-sufficient.
I have no problem with eggs, Mr. Speaker, and I have no problem with dairy products or anything else. Bankers tell me they have no problems with producers in those organizations either, whether provincial or federal. We have done a better job than any other country in the world. In turn this may lead to unproductive competition among provinces.
We must have harmonization of the stabilization programs. There may be restrictions on agricultural products moving within Canada, and difficulties in international trade if some price support levels are judged unfair by our trading partners. As I said earlier today, we must remember that we are one of the largest exporters of cereal grain in proportion to our production. On average, 74 per cent of it goes to world markets. No other country exports such a high percentage of production.
I do not expect an overnight success in reaching harmony among provincial and federal stabilization programs. We have had long discussions on the subject at our federal-provincial meetings in the last two years, without reaching agreement. However, the provincial agricultural ministers are as concerned as I am about the problem, and as anxious as I am to find a solution.
In fact stabilization will be high on the agenda at federal-provincial agricultural talks being held in Ottawa tomorrow and Friday. I can report to the House that Agriculture Canada will be going into these meetings with some new thoughts for a workable compromise.
One of the reasons I am confident we will be more successful in our discussions at this time is that we will not be talking about stabilization in isolation from other problems. Harmonization of stabilization is just one aspect of agricultural development. We will be discussing all our agricultural development programs with the provincial authorities in the months ahead.
In the Speech from the Throne the government stated its intention to work out a more co-ordinated approach to agricultural development. Agricultural development is a cornerstone of the over-all food strategy. My department will be taking the lead in building the new agricultural development strategy. I would like at this time to outline more fully for the members of the House what we will be doing about it.
First, though, I want to dispel the idea that agricultural development is something that affects only farmers. It is a vital matter for each and every Canadian. The strength of the food and agricultural industry affects employment. One in every four Canadian workers owes his employment to the food chain-whether in production, processing, transporting food, retailing, or in industries that supply machinery, energy and other inputs for the food industry. Agricultural development also affects food prices, food quality, and the security and dependability of our food supplies. It affects our international commitments and moral responsibility to supply food aid to areas of the globe less fortunate than ourselves. The decisions

October 26, 1977
The Address-Mr. Whelan
we make about the future directions for our food and agricultural industry will also affect the quality of life in Canada, particularly the sort of life people will lead in our rural areas.
The aim of the government in establishing a strategy for agricultural development is to tap the full potential of the food industry to contribute to the growing Canadian economy. How can we reach this goal?
To begin with, we must set specific objectives. Then we must co-ordinate our efforts to achieve these ends. This means consultation among all the federal departments that have programs to encourage agricultural development. Agriculture Canada will be taking the lead in this consultation process. We will be evaluating all the current development programs. In co-operation with the other federal departments involved, particularly the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, we will assess the impact of current policies on agricultural development. We will see if we need to make changes in these programs and their funding.
Agriculture Canada will then take the lead in meeting with provincial officials to get their response to the federal government's agricultural development goals, and to discuss what separate and joint programs can achieve the best results. Other departments currently negotiating aspects of agricultural development with the provinces will either be turning over these negotiations to Agriculture Canada or involving the agriculture department in joint negotiations or accepting Agriculture Canada's co-ordination input.
One of the most important aspects of the agricultural development strategy is that it will be an approach team with various federal and provincial departments co-operating on development programs. Producer, consumer and industry organizations will also be on the team and will have an important input into these programs. As Minister of Agriculture, I accept my responsibility to be leader of that team.
I have said that our over-all objective in agricultural development is to assist agriculture in realizing its full market potential. Perhaps I should elaborate a little on this theme. There are eight specific objectives we want to achieve.
First, we will aim for increased production efficiency in the Canadian agricultural industry. As you know, Canadian farmers are among the most efficient in the world today. But, we have room for improvement. We could make significant gains in production efficiency if we could increase the rate at which proven technology and management practices were made known to farmers. We may need an on-farm demonstration program to show farmers new equipment and techniques at work. Or perhaps we need some direct assistance to farmers for adopting proven managerial and technical methods in agriculture.
A second objective is to maximize the contribution of agriculture to the Canadian economy by ensuring that our resources are devoted to the commodities with the best market potential. 1 have always been honest with farmers. I am going to tell them if they should be shifting from one commodity to

another. I want to give full information to others in the industry as well, agribusiness and extension workers, for instance, so that they can play a part in helping the industry make necessary adjustments.
Our third objective is to help low income farm families to make a better living in agriculture. Improving farmer efficiency and using agricultural resources to produce the right commodities will no doubt help low income farmers. However, this group has some special problems and we need to make a special effort to overcome them. Maybe the answers will include special training programs, or a program to intensify production on these farms without expanding the land base, or efforts to include part-time farmers in programs that now exclude producers who also work off the farm.
A fourth point we must consider is the conservation and improvement of national agricultural resources. We are already working on a national land-use policy as part of the food strategy development. And we already have programs under PFRA and ARDA to encourage soil and water conservation, drainage improvement, and community resources such as community pastures. But, obviously, these programs can be reviewed and strengthened.
Along with increased efficiency at the farm level, we need increased efficiency in the marketing system. Much is possible in this area. Let me give just a few examples of recent actions by the federal government to improve marketing efficiency. In the area of markets information, Agriculture Canada has evaluated all of its current services and is changing them in response to ideas from users in the industry.
Among the changes introduced, we are offering, starting November 1, a free phone-in national livestock market report, updated daily. Farmers and others in the industry can get this report by calling a Zenith number. Our recently announced program for storage assistance for feed grains in feed grain deficient areas is another example of a service to improve marketing efficiency. Improvements in marketing efficiency will also include initiatives for improvements in the processing, distribution, and retail sectors.
Our sixth specific goal is to protect farmers against income instability and the natural hazards faced in agricultural production. I have already talked about our stabilization policies. However, we must also consider the results of instability on world markets. I think immediately of the beef industry and the beef trade problems we have had to grapple with in the past two years. At the present time, I believe we have the beef trade situation in hand. However, if warranted, we may consider legislation to set up a national meat authority with powers to control exports and imports.
If necessary, I have been authorized by the government to look at the possibility of the passing of a Meat Authority Act, provided I could be assured of the very close collaboration of the opposition.

Oh, oh!
October 26, 1977
You said you wanted it. There is the challenge for you to accept.
Hear, hear!

The horticultural industry is another sector greatly affected by prices and production levels outside Canada. We are studying the whole horticultural sector with a view to improving tariff protection and other assistance that may be necessary to build viable domestic fruit and vegetable industries. Not every fruit and vegetable crop can be produced profitably in Canada in the long run, but we are looking at which ones deserve protection and assistance to reach their potential. This is our seventh specific objective, to provide longer term protection against foreign competition for selected commodities.
The eighth specific objective is to improve access to foreign markets for Canadian agricultural commodities. We can produce more food in this country than we can consume. But we need to be sure of international markets before we produce food products in excess of our domestic requirements. Agriculture Canada, as well as Industry, Trade and Commerce, will be looking at possible new initiatives to promote our agricultural products abroad. The current round of multilateral trade negotiations provides us with the opportunity to improve our over-all access to a number of foreign markets. We have consulted with the various sectors of the food and agricultural industry in developing our negotiating position. Those consultations are still going on.
In working to meet all these objectives, we must keep in mind the significant differences among the various agricultural regions of Canada. They differ both in potential and in problems and we must accommodate regional objectives along with these national ones, as much as possible.
The federal-provincial co-operation on agricultural development and harmonizing stabilization programs will have a considerable impact on national unity. I am confident we will be able to reduce friction between provinces on the stabilization issue. Our new agricultural development strategy will be forged in the interests of the whole nation without overlooking regional problems.
Our efforts to define further the agricultural development strategy will follow the same co-operative process being used to create a total food strategy, that is, the federal government is counting on participation and input from farm organizations, consumer groups, food retailers, the processing and distributing industry and all others involved in the food chain. In addition, the provinces will have a large role in determining the shape of agricultural development programs for the future.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset 1 would like to congratulate the hon. member for Louis-Hebert (Mr. Dawson) and the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. Wood) for their participation in the debate. I, along with many Canadians, felt deeply honoured by the presence of Her Majesty as she participated in the proceedings at the opening of this session of parliament.
I would like to draw the attention of the House to a fairy tale which probably many of us learned about in our younger days. It is a Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale entitled "The Emperor's New Clothes." The story goes something like this.
The emperor loved clothes and spent very little time on matters of state. One day two cheats or charlatans came to the castle and told him they were weavers of the very finest cloth. They asked him if they could weave some cloth for him. He gladly consented.
This went on for some time, and as the days approached when the cloth was to be completed, the emperor sent one of his most trusted ministers to check on the progress of the operation. When the trusted minister got there he looked at the loom, and on it saw nothing. But the two charlatans pointed out the wonderful imaginary pattern in the wonderful cloth that they were weaving. The minister, very concerned about the wrath of the emperor, decided to go back to the emperor and tell him the story the two charlatans had told him.
This went on for some time, Mr. Speaker, until one day the emperor came to look at the cloth that was being woven and he, too, was conned by the very same story his minister had been told.
To put the fairy tale in perspective, the day came when the emperor came to the weavers to put on his new suit of clothes. He took off his clothes and put on his imaginary new clothes. Then, having said there was going to be a great procession through the town, he walked through the town and the courtiers hung on to the imaginary train, until they passed a small child.
The small child, unlike the adults who were looking at the emperor and exulting about his wonderful clothes, simply said, "The emperor has no clothes". And the people said, "Listen to the innocent. The innocent says the emperor has no clothes; indeed, the emperor is naked".
That story, though fairy tale, launches us into the very type of situation in which we Canadians find ourselves today. The throne speech, to many Canadians, was to be the cloth whereby we were going to get a new dimension, a new hope for the future. We find the emperor, who has been the so-called Prime Minister of this country for the last nine years, following the throne speech, and again following his participation in this
The Address-Mr. Epp
debate, is devoid of new ideas. Indeed, the emperor is naked, naked of any direction, and naked of any future hope for Canadians. Surely the Speech from the Throne should be a thrust. It is an opportunity for the government to show Canadians that it is capable of leading. Unfortunately, the Speech from the Throne was devoid of credibility. It gave no hope to Canadians. Much more, Mr. Speaker, once again it placed a wedge between Canadians and those who are to govern, showing there is no trust in the government of the day.
What is the record, Mr. Speaker? In 1968 Canada was united. The euphoria of Expo and of the related Centennial activities was such that it bound Canadians together. Today, whether one assesses our economy or our future as a country, the government gives little cause for hope. Is there any hope for the one million unemployed in Canada? At the present time our unemployment rate is running at approximately 8.3 per cent. Statistics can be very cold; one million unemployed is bad enough, but even more important, when we look at Canadian workers under the age of 25 we find that their unemployment rate is double that of the Canadian average.
It cannot be said any better, Mr. Speaker, than in the words of the Speech from the Throne. This extract is to be found at page 2 of Hansard:
The human hardship imposed by the current level of unemployment in Canada is deeply disturbing. It is neither just nor tolerable that in this country there should be so many men and women deprived of the dignity of self-supporting work, unable to meet their financial commitments and plan confidently for the future. It is intolerable that so many are deprived of their right to secure and productive lives and that their families bear an unfair burden of worry, uncertainty, and deprivation. On a national scale, unemployment now constitutes a very serious obstacle to economic growth.
By their very words, Mr. Speaker, the government stands indicted. The evidence is one million unemployed. Every member of this House knows that, as the winter months come and go, this unemployment rate will increase. What is the government's response? The only response it has given is another make-work project, another $150 million of largesse. That $150 million comes from where, Mr. Speaker? It comes from the taxpayers of Canada. This is but a short-term solution.
We need a better manpower strategy, Mr. Speaker, one which will create an economic climate which is conducive to steady growth. We need to create approximately half a million jobs per year, and this projection is valid until approximately the mid-1980's. At the present time we are creating only about one half of the needed jobs. We will never create those jobs, we will never create that climate, by shor term make-work projects. What is needed is a manpower and industrial strategy whereby the private sector is encouraged and in fact given incentives-not handouts, because that is welfare of another kind-so it will not see everything which it produces taxed away.
I want to get to this point a little later, Mr. Speaker, but I believe that today we have stepped over the boundary of fair taxation and reached the position of confiscation. That is the situation in which we, as Canadians, find ourselves today. We are confiscating much of that which belongs to individual

October 26, 1977
The Address-Mr. Epp
Canadians; it is taken by government and redistributed in a very unequal and unfair manner.
As a western Canadian, Mr. Speaker, I ask for how many years have we argued, begged, and pleaded with the government to bring forward an industrial strategy whereby we will be able more equitably to develop our own agricultural products and commodities? Where is the industrial strategy? Instead, Mr. Speaker, we had the Calgary Conference on Western Economic Opportunities. Western aspirations are no closer to reality today under this government than they were at the time that conference was held in 1973. We need to create jobs, Mr. Speaker, permanent jobs, not government handout jobs. But this government is not going to provide those jobs.
As for productivity, all Canadians who have studied this question know that our standard of living is largely dependent on the fact that we are an exporting nation. Seventy per cent of our trade, both imports and exports, is still with our neighbour to the south, this despite the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has attempted to erode the confidence in and the good relationship that we have had with our neighbour to the south. Our cost of manufacturing is from 20 per cent to 25 per cent higher than it is in the United States. Added to this, the United States has other advantages, such as a more southerly latitude and economy of scale with a population ten times that of ours. So at the best of times it is difficult to penetrate that market. As a result we have lost jobs. Why are we not competitive, Mr. Speaker? It is because we have created an environment of high production costs, whether one talks about wages or whether one talks about taxes.
Another factor which is becoming more and more apparent at this time is that the regulatory agencies, both federal and provincial, are constantly encroaching upon the private sector and adding to those costs. The only way we can finance trade at the present time is by the export in raw form of our agricultural products and very often of our national resource commodities. When the world market goes soft, as we keep hearing is the case today, we lose our competitive advantage.
The world recognizes, Mr. Speaker, that we are in great difficulty. There was an article in the Globe and Mail of September 28, 1977, simply entitled "Japan shocks Davis"- that is Premier Davis-"with a stern rebuke over strikes, taxes". The article went on to refer to our labour force, and then had this to say:
The Japanese business leaders cited higher corporate income taxes in Canada as the second most important reason why Japan looks to the United States.
Lack of productivity has also resulted in lack of investor confidence. Where is investment confidence today? Why is it that Canadians do not want to invest in their own country but rather look to the United States as a better place for their capital? Why is there a flight of capital? I say it is largely due to the lack of economic leadership on the part of this government and successive finance ministers.
In the 1960's, Mr. Speaker, we heard it said more and more that profits were too high. In fact we often hear it said that the word "profits" is a dirty word. One simple fact in our economy is that profits create jobs. Again no leadership has been given

by this government in creating that type of climate. The government's response has been to change its minister of finance. Again I say that the emperor who is to lead has been found naked, devoid of leadership.
As for inflation, Mr. Speaker, granted inflation is a factor in every economy of the western industrial world, the fact of the matter is that inflation rates in Canada today are increasing despite controls. Other countries, including the United Kingdom along with their unemployment rate, have a lower rate than we have. Surely we have become the sick man of the international economic community; it is no longer Britain.
We all remember the Prime Minister saying in 1974, "Zap, you're frozen". To my mind, the reason why the anti-inflation regulations have been ineffective is that the government lacks credibility, because it said one thing in a campaign and then, when politically expedient to do so, said something else.
Governments must tell the truth. When they do not, it is the people who suffer and get a jaundiced and wrong view of governments. Therefore they say that all of us cannot be trusted. The biggest losers in this shell game have been the Canadian people.
What has been the result of this lack of leadership? What about the sliding dollar? It is not sliding any more, it has sunk below 90 cents. It has sunk to the 1932 level at the height of the depression. We must remember that the dollar is 90 cents as against a declining American dollar. It has come to the point where a cartoonist like Ben Wicks portrays two people walking down the street: one is about to pick up a piece of paper, and the other one says: "Frank, don't bother, it is only a Canadian dollar."
We are the laughing stock of the industrial community. As a result, because of our heavy international foreign borrowings, those borrowings are becoming more expensive every day.
The government has shown the greatest lack of leadership in government spending. I am referring to governments at all levels. At this time close to 43 cents out of every dollar, which is made in goods and services, is taken by the three levels of government. In order to put it in practical terms, it means that a Canadian worker earning $15,000 a year will pay direct and hidden taxes in the amount of $6,800. That is what it is like to be a Canadian today.
To put it another way: during January, February, March and to the middle of April, he or she will work in order to pay federal and provincial income taxes. He or she will continue working during the rest of April, all of May and half of June to pay the rest of his or her taxes. On June 15 or 16, finally he or she will be entitled to work for themselves. What has happened to incentive? The government is silently sitting by, hoping it will go away like a bad dream or a bad headache.
I see the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) is in the House today. I have respect for him, but he should be told that he has a big job to do. Unfortunately he does not have a Prime Minister or a cabinet who are willing to say the things that

need to be said, and much more important, are not willing to follow the things that should be said. The Prime Minister is not willing to do this because he is an interventionist into the market place. Ele enjoys it, he wants it, and that is the direction in which he wants to point Canada. All he will do at this point in time, if it is not politically expedient for him to do it, is ease off. The minute it is possible for him to do it politically, he will do it once again.
We have repeatedly heard about the taxpayers, that it is the corporations which are paying the high taxes. The 1975 Canada Year Book indicates that 85 per cent of all working Canadians are individual or salaried earners. These people are the ones who have to pay the shot.
One might say, if we have a 43 per cent level of taxation, that hopefully the in-trust money is being spent well. Is it? What did the Auditor General say in his report? 1 should like to refer to the report of the Auditor General for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1976, which reads in part as follows:
The present state of the financial management and control systems of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is significantly below the acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
Where does the government spend money? The government keeps on asking where we would cut back. In order to give this House an example of where I would cut back, I will refer to an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press and was reprinted by the Winnipeg Chamber of Commerce. It received wide circulation during the recent Manitoba election. When asked the question: "Who is the largest spender in Canadian advertising dollars", one might say General Motors, Ford, or Proctor and Gamble. Elliott Research determined last year that Proctor and Gamble was No. 1. Who is No. 1 today? Today the government of Canada spends more money on advertising than any single corporation in Canada, without taking into consideration the spending of the Crown corporations. Is that restraint? If one were to add to that the spending in advertising by Air Canada, Canadian National Railways or CN Telecommunications, just to name three, what would be the advertising dollars then? A lot of these programs are compulsory.
I should like to refer back to that article and quote from it in part:
It must come as a bit of shock to discover that the advertising cost of programs such as persuading Canadians that filling out income tax forms-already required by law-can be fun, or telling everyone, at a cost which exceeded that of energy saved, that Environment Canada is really an energy miser after all . ..
Today the Government of Canada consumes more money than does Simpsons-Sears, Bell Canada, the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, Dominion Stores, Nabisco, Pepsi-Cola, and the Royal Bank of Canada combined to sell their wares. One must remember that these firms are competing businesses. On the other hand, the Canadian Post Office, which has a monopoly, considers it necessary to spend $350,000 to improve its image, a task that would be more readily accomplished if the money were spent to improve service.
One can refer to the ministerial use of aircraft. That was brought forward once again in this session of parliament. The
The Address-Mr. Epp
people of Canada will be conned no longer. They will not be bought by their own money. The evidence of that is what happened in Manitoba during the election last week. Prior to that election the campaign strategy was very simple. The campaign strategy of the Progressive Conservative party, which has now been sworn in as the government of Manitoba, was that we would run on a policy of restraint. For many people that was not a very popular move. They said that people must be given promises. We said that Canadian people, and specifically the people of Manitoba, were not willing to be conned; tell them the truth and they will respond.
Apparently the press did not believe us. On October 3, 1977, an article appeared in the Financial Times of Canada by Roger Newman. That article was entitled: "PCs Hopeful but Unlikely in Manitoba Vote". I should like to quote the last paragraph of that article, which reads as follows:
If the vote was held today, most observers think Manitobans would elect a minority NDP government, with perhaps a weaker Tory contingent as the official opposition and the Liberals as a fairly strong third party. Since no dramatic issues are being debated, the parties could end up in something close to a three-way tie, with the result that a rematch might be necessary within a year.
What is that non-dramatic issue of which Mr. Newman speaks? It is that we said to Manitoba that spending must stop and taxation must be reduced. Also we said that there would be six taxes we would eliminate, one of which was succession duty.
I asked the Minister of Finance the other day whether he would follow the lead of the Manitoba government, whereby a farmer or an owner of a small family owned business would be able to transfer or sell, without the penalty of capital gains, to a close family member once during his lifetime. I am in agreement with that because it would enable the family to retain the family farm or business.
As 1 have said before, we have gone beyond the threshold of fair taxation to confiscation. This government is confiscating the rightful property of Canadian taxpayers. These family farms and businesses have been paid for; taxes have been paid on those farms and businesses, and yet the government wants capital gains. The government complains about youth leaving the farms and not carrying on with their fathers' businesses. The reason is very simple: confiscation.
We must return to living in a society with incentives. We live in a technological age, and we must adjust to that age. The Minister of Finance should reduce government spending on non-productive sectors such as advertising and direct more money into research and development.
Let us put research and development on a better footing in order that the technology with which we can develop can be used for the creation of new jobs in the technological age. My concern today is especially for the transportation industry and for energy.
Not only is the economic situation such that the emperor is naked, he is also devoid of any new ideas with respect to Canadian unity. We will never solve the question of Canadian

The Address-Mr. Epp
unity so long as the regions feel they are outside the decisionmaking process in the country. That is what we feel in western Canada. I do not want to speak only as a western Canadian-I want to speak as a Canadian-but there are regions in Canada which feel they are being left out, and the government must wake up to it. There is a close link between the economic stength of the country and the desire of Canadians to remain within the country, and the unity question will have to be solved.
References have also been made in the House to the language law. Let me say clearly to all members here that, as a Manitoban, 1 do not apologize for what has been done in Manitoba because Manitoba has always had the reputation of being an ethnic province, and as ethnics and citizens of that province all we ask for is equality. We do not ask for a special status or for special rights. All we ask for is equality, and it is time that the government woke up to the fact and announced that all Canadians are equal and that there are not some who are more equal than others.
The same thing applies to a referendum or to any new organization on the constitutional level. We want no special deals, no special status for anyone or for any region of Canada. Unity will not be the product or the outgrowth solely of a change in the economic fortunes of Canada or of constitutional changes but, rather, as was said in the throne speech read by Her Majesty:
This discontent in such a wealthy country must find its causes in the human spirit, and it is there also that the unity of the nation must be found.
If 1 were to condemn the government for anything-and I would not even refer to the economic situation which is bleak, and I have painted the picture to describe it, nor to Canadian unity which has been destroyed by the Prime Minister during his ten years in office-it would be for its lack of moral leadership, its lack in human spirit.
I want to quote from the speech given to the Canadian Club on October 17, by His Royal Highness the Duke of Edinburgh. He said:
The age of the social conscience, social justice and concern seems to have coincided with the age of crime, pornography, mugging and international terrorism. What started out as a liberalization of restrictive social conventions seems to have developed into a dictatorship of licence.
This dictatorship of licence has gripped Canada. It has not only gripped Canada but it has gripped the western world. I do not want to miss any words when I say that one of the reasons for the malaise which we are experiencing today is that the Prime Minister has tried to destroy many of the moral values on which this country was founded because, with a humanistic approach to life man becomes all important, man becomes the only one, he becomes the 1. All values based on Christian principles are set aside once you put I in the centre of things, and this Prime Minister has done it. That is why we are experiencing this malaise.
The Prime Minister has frequently been in the vanguard of change, and, I say very directly to you, change for the worse, not for the better. Under the guise of civil libertarianism, we thought we would gain greater civil liberty, but civil liberty

has been replaced by licence. For these three reasons alone it is high time that the government packed its bags and left because Canada cannot afford another term of Pierre Elliott Trudeau. I say to you very clearly: Canadians awake. It is time, and the time will come at the next election.
